_doc: What every monster family is weak to, resists and shrugs off, and what its nature refuses or falls to easily, decided from its LORE (winning-build plan 2026-11-13 section 3.2; Brandon: 'lore, not floor'). tools/content/affinity_pass.py --write writes it into data/monsters.json (`weaknesses`, `resistances`, `shrugs_off`, `status_immune`, `status_weak`); data/affinity_rules.json holds the steps (weak x2, resisted x0.5, shrugs off x0.25, cap x3). tests/test_affinity_lore.py checks every family has a profile with a lore note and a source, that monsters.json matches this file, and that every lock has a key above it.

_schema.layers: A kind's profile is its family's, then its group's (if it is in one), then its own (kinds), then the tag rules. FORM (slash, pierce, blunt) comes wholly from the layers: each layer may set a form to weak, resist, shrugs_off or neutral, later layers winning. A named foe (boss, mini-boss, seal demon) keeps the forms written on it in monsters.json unless `kinds` names its form. ELEMENTS and SUBSTANCES (fire, holy, silver, iron...) start from the kind's own lists in monsters.json: a family or tag rule adds softly (never against the kind's own opposite word), a group or kind adds by force (it moves the type from the opposite list); `drop` removes a type from all three lists. STATUS lists: a group's or kind's list, when given, replaces its family's; the tag rules then add to status_immune and take what is immune out of status_weak.
_schema.status_immune: the effect never takes hold, and the game says why (Monster.add_effect, affinity.status_line)
_schema.status_weak: it takes hold without a big foe's resist roll and lasts half again as long; the token fear_of_fire means a fire hit puts it to flight (not on a kind that resists fire)
_schema.holy: holy weakness is for the unholy only: the tags in unholy.tags, and the cursed kinds named in unholy.cursed. Every other kind loses holy from its weaknesses.

unholy.lore: Holy power burns what has turned against heaven: the dead who will not lie down, the fiends of the pit, and the few whose own nature is a curse. A blessed blade against an honest bear is only a blade.
unholy.source: The Christian rite of exorcism (holy water and the sign of the cross against demons and the restless dead); the plan's ruling, section 3.2: 'Holy is narrowed to the unholy (undead, demons, the cursed)'.

cursed.werewolf: Lycaon served Zeus human flesh and was turned into a wolf for it: lycanthropy is a curse.
cursed.werewolf_alpha: Sigmund and Sinfjotli put on cursed wolf skins and could not take them off for ten days.
cursed.elder_werewolf: The oldest of the cursed: the wolf has long since eaten the man.
cursed.wererat: A cursed man, as every were-beast is.
cursed.weretiger: The harimau jadian is a man cursed to become a tiger after dark.
cursed.corrupted_angel: One of the third of the stars the dragon's tail swept from heaven (Revelation 12:4): fallen.
cursed.pegasus_corrupted: A creature of heaven turned rotten: holy light burns what it fell from.
cursed.unicorn_corrupted: The unicorn's horn cleansed poisoned pools; this one's horn poisons them.
cursed.nothic: The curse that answers a wizard's greed bent him into this shape.
cursed.ker: The Keres are the death-spirits of the battlefield, gorging on the blood of the fallen (Hesiod, Shield of Heracles).
cursed.lamia: Grief and Hera's curse turned a queen into a devourer of children.
cursed.bone_golem: A necromancer built it from the bones of the dead and bound it with death-magic.
cursed.gnoll_fang_of_yeenoghu: Marked by the demon lord Yeenoghu: his taint runs in its blood.
cursed.gnoll_alpha_of_yeenoghu: It ate the demon-tainted flesh of the alpha before it.
cursed.mere_wife: The Beowulf poet names Grendel's kin the race of Cain, whom the Creator outlawed and condemned.

undead.lore: The dead do not sleep, and poison has no living blood to ride; they feel no affection for a charm to win (a hero with the Helm of Aragorn's oath is the one exception: Monster.resists_control).
undead.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): the undead are immune to sleep, charm and poison.

demon.lore: Fiends of the pit: holy power burns them.
demon.source: The rite of exorcism; Revelation 20 (the devil cast into the lake of fire).

construct.lore: A made thing has no mind to frighten, muddle or charm, never sleeps and has no blood for poison.
construct.source: The golem of Prague (Rabbi Judah Loew's clay servant) obeys the word on its brow and nothing else.

plant.lore: A plant has no mind to frighten, charm or confuse, and no eyes to blind.
plant.source: Natural history; the old rule of Monster.resists_control, now written down.

elemental.lore: Living fire, stone, wind and water: nothing in them sleeps or can be poisoned.
elemental.source: Paracelsus, A Book on Nymphs, Sylphs, Pygmies and Salamanders (1566): the elemental beings are made of their element alone.

fey.lore: Iron is the fairies' bane: an iron knife in the cradle or a horseshoe over the door keeps them off.
fey.source: British and Irish folk belief, recorded by W. B. Yeats, Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry (1888), and Katharine Briggs, A Dictionary of Fairies (1976).

restless_dead.lore: Walking corpses have no blood to lose and no heart to stop, so a thrust finds nothing to kill. The old way is to take the head.
restless_dead.source: Grettis saga, ch. 35: Grettir wrestles the draugr Glámr, cuts off his head and burns the body.

ghosts.lore: A blade passes through a ghost as through mist: every ordinary blow is mostly wasted. Holy power and fire are what lay them.
ghosts.source: Shakespeare, Hamlet 1.1: the Ghost 'is, as the air, invulnerable, and our vain blows malicious mockery.'

vampires_liches.lore: A vampire is killed with a stake through the heart: a thrust is the way.
vampires_liches.source: Bram Stoker, Dracula (1897), ch. 16: Arthur drives the stake through Lucy's heart.

demons.lore: Fiends of the pit wear flesh like a coat; blades bite it as they bite any flesh. What hurts them is holy power and cold iron.
demons.source: Medieval exorcism manuals (holy water); cold iron against spirits in British folk belief (Katharine Briggs, A Dictionary of Fairies).

dragons.lore: Dragon scales turn a sword's edge, but a thrust finds the gap: Bard's black arrow found the bare patch on Smaug's breast, and Sigurd stabbed Fafnir from below. Dragons breathe fire and do not burn, and they sleep deeply on their gold.
dragons.source: Volsunga saga, ch. 18 (Sigurd in the pit); Tolkien, The Hobbit (1937), ch. 14 (the black arrow); Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 4: Medea sings the sleepless dragon of the Golden Fleece to sleep.

giants.lore: Giants are mighty and slow-witted, and the stories are full of small heroes who trick them into fighting each other.
giants.source: Jack the Giant Killer (English fairy tale): Jack throws stones at two sleeping giants until each thinks the other struck him; Odyssey 9: 'Nobody' blinds the Cyclops.

goblinkin.lore: Goblins, orcs, kobolds and gnolls are flesh and leather like men: no lore lock, no secret key. Their strength is numbers and their war-bands.
goblinkin.source: Tolkien, The Hobbit (1937): the goblins of the Misty Mountains fall to plain swords (Orcrist and Glamdring) like any foe.

mortals.lore: Men and women: what hurts any of us hurts them. Their armour is the only thing that changes the blow.
mortals.source: Common sense, and every war ever fought.

fair_folk.lore: The fair folk fear iron. They are clever and quick, and an ordinary blade cuts them like anyone else, but iron burns them.
fair_folk.source: Yeats, Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry (1888); Briggs, A Dictionary of Fairies (1976).

great_beasts.lore: Wolves, bears, lions and boars are flesh and fur, and every beast fears fire: a torch keeps the pack off.
great_beasts.source: Kipling, The Jungle Book (1894), 'Mowgli's Brothers': Mowgli drives off Shere Khan and the wolves with the Red Flower, fire.

vermin.lore: Rats, bats, beetles and spiders: small enough that the right blow ends them. A beetle's shell turns an edge but cracks under a boot; a swarm cannot be cut at all.
vermin.source: Natural history (an insect's armour is its outer shell); the Pied Piper of Hamelin, for the rats' weakness for a tune.

serpents.lore: Snakes, lizards and frogs are flesh and scale; the old snake charmers sway a cobra with a tune.
serpents.source: Psalm 58:4-5 ('the deaf adder ... which will not hearken to the voice of charmers'); the snake charmers of India and Egypt.

birds.lore: Birds are light and hollow-boned: an arrow brings them down.
birds.source: Apollodorus, Library 2.5.6: Heracles scares the Stymphalian birds up with a bronze rattle and shoots them down.

gorgons.lore: The gorgons and the basilisks kill with a look. Perseus took Medusa's head with a curved sword, looking only at her reflection.
gorgons.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 4; Pliny, Natural History 8.33 (the basilisk).

legend.lore: The monsters of the old stories each fell in their own way, and each one's weakness is its story: see the kinds.
legend.source: Apollodorus, Library (the Labours of Heracles); Hesiod, Theogony.

shapeshifters.lore: A shapeshifter's body is not quite real: wounds close almost as fast as they are made. Its curse has a key.
shapeshifters.source: European folk belief about the were-beasts (see the werewolves group).

constructs.lore: Things of bronze, iron, clay and stone: a blade skates off them or sticks fast, but a hammer cracks them.
constructs.source: The golem of Prague (clay) and Hephaestus's bronze Talos (Apollonius, Argonautica 4); a smith's sense of metal and stone.

elementals.lore: Living fire, air and water close behind a blade like a wound that was never there; stone turns it. The hammer and the opposing element are what break them.
elementals.source: Paracelsus, A Book on Nymphs, Sylphs, Pygmies and Salamanders (1566); the Sumerian poem Lugal-e (Ninurta's mace Sharur breaks the stone army of Asag).

oozes.lore: A jelly closes round a thrust and a blow only wobbles it. Only an edge, cold or fire really harms it, and some jellies split when cut.
oozes.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): the gelatinous cube, the black pudding (cutting divides it) and the oozes; they are blind and mindless.

aberrations.lore: Things from outside the world, each made wrong in its own way: see the kinds.
aberrations.source: Lovecraft's star-spawn and the Dungeons & Dragons aberrations (the beholder, the mind flayer, the mimic).

plants.lore: An arrow sticks in a trunk and does nothing; an axe fells it, and fire takes it. Dry wood goes up like kindling.
plants.source: The woodsman's trade; Tolkien gives the Ents the same dread of axe and fire (The Two Towers, 1954).

celestials.lore: Heaven's own: what they fear is shadow and the death-magic, not holy power.
celestials.source: Revelation; Dionysius the Areopagite, The Celestial Hierarchy.

skeletons.lore: Bones snap under a mace, but a blade slides off them and a thrust goes between the ribs and finds nothing.
skeletons.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): 'sharp and/or edged weapons do only half damage to skeletons; blunt weapons do normal damage.'

armoured.lore: Plate turns a sword's edge and most points; the mace and the war hammer were made for men in plate.
armoured.source: Medieval arms: the flanged mace and the war hammer spread across Europe with plate armour in the fourteenth century.

shades.lore: The wholly bodiless dead: no flesh at all, only cold and shadow. Ordinary blows pass straight through.
shades.source: Homer, Odyssey 11: three times Odysseus tried to embrace his mother's shade, and three times she slipped from his arms like a shadow or a dream.

liches.lore: A lich has put its death outside its body, so blades and points do it little harm. Its bones still break.
liches.source: The Russian tale of Koschei the Deathless (Afanasyev): his death is hidden in a needle, in an egg, in a duck, in a hare, in a chest under an oak.

devils.lore: The devils of the deeper pits fear silver, the pure metal, as witches do.
devils.source: English and German folk belief: silver drives off the Devil and witches (the silver bullet or the silver sixpence); Dungeons & Dragons gives the devils the same weakness.

mimics.lore: A mimic's skin oozes a glue stronger than pitch: a club or a mace sticks fast and does little.
mimics.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): the mimic and its adhesive.

beholders.lore: The great central eye is the beholder's heart and its weakness: a thrust or an arrow into it, or a blinding.
beholders.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): the beholder.

mind_flayers.lore: Masters of the mind cannot be muddled or charmed by a lesser one.
mind_flayers.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): the mind flayer.

earth_elementals.lore: Stone turns any edge or point, and shatters under a hammer.
earth_elementals.source: The Sumerian poem Lugal-e: Ninurta smashes the stone warriors of Asag with his mace Sharur.

fire_elementals.lore: A creature made of fire is not hurt by fire at all, or nearly so. A blade passes through the flame; cold kills it.
fire_elementals.source: Paracelsus (1566): the salamanders live in fire as fish live in water.

water_elementals.lore: You cannot cut, stab or crush water. Lightning and cold go through it.
water_elementals.source: Paracelsus (1566): the undines, the beings of water.

jinn.lore: The jinn, made of smokeless fire, are driven off by iron.
jinn.source: Arab folk belief (the cry 'Hadid! Iron!' against the jinn, recorded by Edward Lane, The Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians, 1836); Qur'an 55:15 (the jinn made of smokeless fire).

jellies.lore: Some jellies flow round an edge too; only fire and cold really harm them.
jellies.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): the ochre jelly.

beetles.lore: A beetle's shell turns an edge but cracks under a hammer or a boot.
beetles.source: Natural history: an insect's armour is its hard outer shell, strong against a cut and brittle to a crushing blow.

swarms.lore: A swarm is ten thousand small things: a blade or a point kills two and misses the rest, and stamping does little better. Fire is the answer, as the hot brand is for rot grubs.
swarms.source: Natural history (the locust plagues of Exodus 10); Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): rot grubs are killed by fire on the skin.

trolls.lore: A troll's wounds close as you watch, unless they are burned or eaten by acid; fire also frightens it.
trolls.source: Poul Anderson, Three Hearts and Three Lions (1961): the troll whose severed parts crawl back together until they are burned; Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): fire and acid stop a troll's regeneration.

cyclopes.lore: A one-eyed giant has one eye to put out: a thrust is its undoing.
cyclopes.source: Homer, Odyssey 9: Odysseus drives a sharpened olive stake into Polyphemus's eye.

werewolves.lore: A were-beast's wounds close almost as fast as they are made; only silver and holy power hurt it properly.
werewolves.source: European folk belief, fixed by the film The Wolf Man (1941): only silver kills the werewolf; Ovid, Metamorphoses 1 (Lycaon cursed into a wolf).

elves.lore: Elves do not sleep as men do, and magic cannot put them to sleep.
elves.source: Tolkien's sleepless Elves; Dungeons & Dragons, Player's Handbook (2014): Fey Ancestry ('magic can't put you to sleep').

snakes.lore: A true snake sways to a charmer's tune and can be charmed out of striking.
snakes.source: Psalm 58:4-5 ('the voice of charmers'); the snake charmers of India.

world_serpents.lore: The Midgard Serpent's children: Thor's hammer is the blow that kills them.
world_serpents.source: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 51: at Ragnarok Thor kills Jormungandr with Mjolnir.

medusas.lore: Perseus took Medusa's head with one stroke of a curved sword: a cutting blow is her undoing.
medusas.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 4; Apollodorus, Library 2.4.2 (the harpe Hermes gave Perseus).

hydras.lore: Cut off one head and two grow back, unless the stump is burned.
hydras.source: Apollodorus, Library 2.5.2: Iolaus sears each stump with a torch as Heracles cuts.

chimeras.lore: Bellerophon killed the Chimera with a lead-tipped spear thrust into its fiery throat: the fire melted the lead.
chimeras.source: John Tzetzes, scholia on Lycophron (the lead-tipped spear); Hesiod, Theogony 319-325.

angels.lore: Heaven's soldiers know no fear and give no love for a charm to win.
angels.source: Revelation 12:7: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon.

hags.lore: The old hags sit on sleepers' chests; they know every trick of sleep and cannot be lulled.
hags.source: The Old Hag of Newfoundland and the mare of Germanic folklore, who rides the sleeper's chest.

wood_golem.lore: Wood is felled by an axe: a cutting blow is what it fears, and fire.

flesh_golem.lore: Stitched from the dead: a thrust finds no vitals, but a cut opens the seams.

homunculus.lore: A foot-tall man of the maker's own blood: small and soft, no harder to hurt than a cat.
homunculus.source: Paracelsus, De Natura Rerum (1537): the homunculus grown in a flask.

talos.lore: Talos was bronze from head to foot, except for one vein from his neck to his ankle, sealed with a single bronze nail. An arrow in the ankle let his ichor out.
talos.source: Apollodorus, Library 1.9.26: Poeas shot Talos in the ankle (or Medea pulled the nail).

bronze_sentinel.lore: A guard built on Talos's pattern, with Talos's flaw: one point where a thrust gets in.

crystal_ooze.lore: Its jelly has gone to crystal, and crystal shatters.

black_pudding.lore: A cutting blow divides a black pudding into two smaller ones; it does not resist the edge, it multiplies under it.
black_pudding.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): slashing and lightning split the black pudding.

gas_spore.lore: A floating puffball full of spores: one thrust pops it.
gas_spore.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): the gas spore.

brown_mold.lore: Brown mold drinks heat: fire feeds it, so it never catches.
brown_mold.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Dungeon Masters Guide (1979): brown mold grows from fire.

corrupted_treant.lore: A whole oak gone bad: blows and arrows hardly mark it, but an axe still fells it.
corrupted_treant.source: Tolkien, The Two Towers (1954): the Ents and the axe.

moss_sentinel.lore: A mound of moss over a frame of roots and stone: a blow sinks in, an edge cuts it free.

nemean_lion.lore: No blade or arrow could pierce the Nemean lion's hide. Heracles stunned it with his club and strangled it.

calydonian_boar.lore: Atalanta's arrow drew first blood and Meleager's spear killed it; swords glanced off its bristles.

hell_bovine.lore: The cows of the secret level shrug off a club: their hide is thick as a barn door.
hell_bovine.source: Diablo II (2000): the Secret Cow Level.

stymphalian_bird.lore: Heracles scared the bronze-feathered birds up with a rattle that Athena gave him.

sown_warrior.lore: The Spartoi sprang from the dragon's teeth. Cadmus threw a stone among them, and each thought another had struck him: they killed each other.

echidna.lore: Argus All-Eyes killed Echidna as she slept.

jiangshi.lore: A hopping corpse is stopped dead by a Taoist priest's paper talisman stuck to its forehead.
jiangshi.source: Chinese folk belief, made famous by the film Mr. Vampire (1985).

grave_guardian.lore: Buried standing at the crypt door after swearing to keep holy ground: the blessing on them still holds, so holy power does not burn them.

undead_colossus.lore: A hill of stitched corpses: a blow sinks into it, but an axe hacks it apart.

flesh_colossus.lore: A hill of stitched flesh: a blow sinks into it, but an axe hacks it apart.

hrungnirs_ghost.lore: Hrungnir's heart and head were stone. Thor's hammer shattered the giant's whetstone and his skull.

mere_wife.lore: Beowulf's sword Hrunting would not bite on Grendel's mother; only the giant-forged blade from her own hall killed her.

cave_troll.lore: A cave troll's hide is like stone: a club rebounds from it.
cave_troll.source: Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring (1954): the troll in Moria.

ettin_warchief.lore: Two heads, one thick skull each: a club does little, but an edge or a point gets in.

sobek_warrior.lore: Crocodile hide turns a cutting blow.
sobek_warrior.source: Natural history: the crocodile's bony scutes.

mud_crawler.lore: Its scales turn a cutting blow.

gibbering_mouther.lore: A heap of mouths and eyes in loose flesh: a blow sinks into it.
gibbering_mouther.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual II (1983): the gibbering mouther.

lurking_horror.lore: A shapeless thing that closes round a thrust.

chaos_spawn.lore: A scrap of first Chaos: an edge or a blow meets nothing that stays put.

girtablilu.lore: The scorpion-men of Mashu wear a scorpion's armour: blade and point skate off, a mace cracks it.
girtablilu.source: The Epic of Gilgamesh, tablet IX: the scorpion-men at the mountain gate.

charybdis.lore: A whirlpool with a mouth: a blow is swallowed by the water.

charybdis_spawn.lore: A little whirlpool with a mouth: a blow is swallowed by the water.

the_sphinx.lore: Oedipus beat her with an answer; in the old pictures heroes go at the sphinx with a spear.
the_sphinx.source: Sophocles, Oedipus Rex; Greek vase paintings of the sphinx and the spear.

lava_elemental.lore: Molten rock: a hammer splashes through it, a point melts.

green_knight.lore: Gawain took the Green Knight's head with one stroke, and the knight picked it up and rode away: a cutting blow does not trouble him.
green_knight.source: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (14th century).

wild_hunt_captain.lore: A rider of the sky-hunt: half of him is storm.

lyssa_madness.lore: Lyssa is madness itself; nothing can muddle her.
lyssa_madness.source: Euripides, Heracles: Hera sends Lyssa to drive Heracles mad.

pixie_swarm.lore: A cloud of finger-high pranksters dodging every blade.
pixie_swarm.source: Devon and Cornwall folk belief (being pixy-led).

khrafstra_swarm.lore: A seething knot of the evil spirit's vermin: no blow of any kind does much to it. Fire does.
khrafstra_swarm.source: The Zoroastrian Vendidad: the khrafstra, the noxious creatures.

ice_elemental.lore: Living ice: an edge or a point skates off it, and a hammer shatters it.
ice_elemental.source: Paracelsus (1566): the elemental beings; the plain physics of ice.

world_serpent.lore: Jormungandr's scales turn blade and point alike; Thor's hammer is the blow that kills him.

pit_executioner.lore: The headsman of the pit wears a hide of black iron that turns an edge.

risen_deadite.lore: A deadite risen again: rotten bone that a club breaks apart.
risen_deadite.source: The Evil Dead films (1981-1992): the deadites are hacked and smashed apart.

dahaka_wyrm.lore: Fereydun struck down Zahhak with his ox-headed mace; a cut or a thrust only lets out the vermin inside him.
dahaka_wyrm.source: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh (Fereydun and the ox-headed mace); the Avesta (Azhi Dahaka full of noxious creatures).

tiamat.lore: Marduk drove the winds into Tiamat's mouth and shot an arrow that split her belly.
